title: Spain
description: Auden's Spanish Civil War poem: 'History to the defeated / May say Alas but cannot help or pardon'.
plot_or_argument: The poem is a brief history of Spain and of the struggle, from the prehistoric to the present, ending with the famous lines on the necessary struggle and the ambiguous consolation of history.
narrative_structure: A short pamphlet poem in sections, published by Faber as a sixpenny pamphlet.
historical_context: The Spanish Civil War of 1936–39, the International Brigades, and the political crisis of the British left.
literary_significance: Spain is the central political poem of the 1930s and Auden's most controversial work: its rhetoric of the necessary struggle made it the anthem of the left, and Auden's later repudiation of its 'wicked doctrine' is one of the period's revealing gestures.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Faber and Faber in 1937 as a pamphlet; Auden suppressed the poem after 1939 and it was excluded from his Collected Poems.

title: Another Time
description: The last collection of Auden's English years: 'September 1, 1939', 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' and the farewell to England.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats', 'September 1, 1939', 'Musée des Beaux Arts', 'The Unknown Citizen', 'Refugee Blues' and 'Law Like Love' — the great public poems of 1939 and the farewell to the England he was leaving.
historical_context: The Munich crisis, the fall of Czechoslovakia, the outbreak of the Second World War, and Auden's emigration to America in January 1939.
literary_significance: Another Time contains the two most quoted poems of 1939 and the definitive elegy of the period: 'In Memory of W. B. Yeats' — 'poetry makes nothing happen' — and 'September 1, 1939' gave the outbreak of the war its permanent lines.

title: Lions and Shadows: An Education in the Twenties
description: Isherwood's account of his Cambridge and Berlin years, and the most entertaining memoir of the twenties.
plot_or_argument: Isherwood recounts his childhood, his years at Cambridge, his medical studies, his time as a tutor and his first journey to Berlin, and sketches the friends and masters who made his education — with a lightly disguised portrait of Auden, 'Hugh Weston'.
narrative_structure: A chronological memoir of education from childhood to Berlin.
principal_characters: Isherwood; 'Hugh Weston' (Auden); the friends and masters
historical_context: Cambridge in the 1920s, the literary London of the period, and the first journey to Berlin.
literary_significance: Lions and Shadows is the most entertaining memoir of the twenties and one of the finest English autobiographies of education: its portrait of the young Auden and its comic account of the formation of a writer made it a period classic.

title: Goodbye to Berlin
description: The definitive English book about Weimar Berlin, and the source of Cabaret: 'I am a camera'.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, an English writer in Berlin from 1930 to 1933, records the boarding house of Fräulein Schroeder, the cabaret singer Sally Bowles, the Jewish family Landauer, the working-class Nowaks and the rise of the Nazis — and leaves as Hitler comes to power.
narrative_structure: Six linked stories narrated by an English observer, from 1930 to 1933.
principal_characters: The narrator; Sally Bowles; Fräulein Schroeder; Natalia Landauer; Bernhard Landauer; Otto Nowak
historical_context: Berlin from 1930 to 1933, the last years of the Weimar Republic, the cabaret and the boarding house, and the Nazi seizure of power.
literary_significance: Goodbye to Berlin is the definitive English book about Weimar Berlin and one of the great documentaries of the period: its camera-eye narration, its portrait of Sally Bowles and its record of the Nazi rise became the source of Cabaret and the century's image of the doomed city.

title: Autumn Journal
description: The finest long poem of the thirties: a poetic diary from the autumn of 1938 to the spring of 1939.
plot_or_argument: The poem records the months from October 1938 to the spring of 1939: the Munich crisis, the fear of war, a journey to Spain and Ireland, the death of MacNeice's mother, and the ordinary life of London — in a conversational, rhymed, sectioned meditation.
narrative_structure: Twenty-four numbered sections in rhymed verse, from October 1938 to the spring of 1939.
principal_characters: MacNeice; his mother; his wife; the people of London and Spain
historical_context: The Munich crisis of September 1938, the outbreak of the Second World War, the Spanish Civil War, and Ireland.
literary_significance: Autumn Journal is the finest long poem of the thirties and one of the great poems of the period: its conversational tone, its rhyme and its record of the last months of peace made it the definitive poetic diary of the decade.

title: The Burning Perch
description: MacNeice's last collection: 'The Taxis', 'Charon' and the dark lyric of the nuclear age.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Taxis', 'Charon', 'Hold the Sun in Your Hands', 'The Introduction' and the poems of loss and death that made it MacNeice's finest late book.
historical_context: The Cold War and the nuclear threat, MacNeice's years at the BBC, and the death of his second wife.
literary_significance: The Burning Perch is MacNeice's finest late collection: its dark lyric and its poems of death are among the best English poems of the postwar period.

title: Poems (Spender, 1933)
description: Spender's first major collection: 'The Pylons', 'The Express' and the public lyric of the thirties.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Pylons', 'The Express', 'Not Palaces', 'I Think Continually of Those Who Were Truly Great' and the poems of the machine, the modern landscape and the political crisis.
narrative_structure: A collection of lyrics and longer poems.
historical_context: The England of the early 1930s, the pylons and the railway, and the political awakening of the decade.
literary_significance: Spender's Poems gave the thirties its most lyrical public voice: 'The Pylons' and 'The Express' are the definitive poems of the machine in the English landscape, and 'I Think Continually' is one of the best-known poems of the period.

title: Vienna
description: Spender's poem of the Austrian crisis: the failure of the left and the coming of fascism.
plot_or_argument: The sequence records the Austrian civil war of February 1934 and the defeat of the Social Democrats in Vienna, in verse and prose, as the first defeat of the European left before fascism.
narrative_structure: A sequence of poems and prose passages.
historical_context: The Austrian civil war of February 1934, the rise of Dollfuss and the fascist movements of central Europe.
literary_significance: Vienna is the most politically direct poem of the Auden generation: its account of the defeat of the Viennese left made it the period's clearest statement about the failure of the European left before fascism.

title: World Within World
description: One of the great English memoirs of the century: the thirties, Spain, the Auden circle and the war.
plot_or_argument: Spender recounts his childhood, Oxford and the Auden circle, the Spanish Civil War, his marriage and his homosexuality, the Second World War and the literary world of the period.
narrative_structure: A chronological autobiography covering childhood to the postwar years.
principal_characters: Spender; Auden; Isherwood; MacNeice; the Spanish war
historical_context: Oxford in the late 1920s, the Auden circle, the Spanish Civil War and the English literary world of the thirties and forties.
literary_significance: World Within World is one of the great English autobiographies of the century: its record of the Auden generation, of Spain and of the literary politics of the period made it an indispensable document of the thirties.

title: Homage to Catalonia
description: Orwell's Spain: the Barcelona militias, the betrayal of the revolution and a bullet through the throat.
plot_or_argument: Orwell goes to Spain in 1936 to fight for the Republic, joins the POUM militia on the Aragon front, and experiences the revolutionary Barcelona of the first months; in May 1937 he is caught in the street fighting between the Communists and the anarchists, and later shot through the neck. The book ends with his escape from Spain and his anger at the left's complicity in the suppression of the revolution.
narrative_structure: Thirteen chapters in a chronological account, with two political appendices.
principal_characters: Orwell; Georges Kopp; the POUM militia; the Communist press
historical_context: The Spanish Civil War (1936–39), the Barcelona May Days of 1937, the Communist suppression of the POUM and the anarchists, and the political dishonesty of the British left.
literary_significance: Homage to Catalonia is the finest English book on the Spanish Civil War and the founding text of Orwell's political honesty: its account of revolutionary Barcelona and of the left's betrayal of its own cause is unmatched.

title: Burmese Days
description: Orwell's first novel and the great English novel of the empire: a colonial club in Burma and the rot at its heart.
plot_or_argument: John Flory, a timber merchant in a small Burmese town, is a lonely, liberal Englishman with a Burmese mistress and a birthmark; he befriends the Indian doctor Veraswami and tries to prevent the elevation of the corrupt U Po Kyin to the club, but is destroyed by the racism, gossip and hypocrisy of the colonial community.
narrative_structure: Chronological third-person narrative in twenty-five chapters.
principal_characters: John Flory; Elizabeth Lackersteen; Veraswami; U Po Kyin; Ma Hla May; Mr Lackersteen
historical_context: British Burma in the 1920s, the colonial club, the timber trade, and the racial hierarchy of the empire.
literary_significance: Burmese Days is the great English novel of the empire and the finest thing Orwell wrote before his nonfiction: its portrait of the colonial club and its diagnosis of imperial racism made it the most honest English novel about the empire before A Passage to India's successors.

title: Keep the Aspidistra Flying
description: Orwell's novel of the bookshop and the money-god: a poet's war against respectability.
plot_or_argument: Gordon Comstock, a would-be poet from a respectable family, gives up a good job to work in a bookshop and wage war on the 'money god'; he sinks into poverty, loses his girlfriend Rosemary and nearly destroys himself, and the novel ends with his surrender to marriage, a job and the aspidistra in the window.
narrative_structure: Chronological narrative in the third person, ending in compromise.
principal_characters: Gordon Comstock; Rosemary Waterlow; Philip Ravelston; Julia Comstock; Mr Cheeseman
historical_context: London in the 1930s, the book trade, the genteel poor and the cult of respectability.
literary_significance: Keep the Aspidistra Flying is Orwell's finest novel of the 1930s and the great English novel about money: its portrait of the genteel poor and its analysis of the money-god made it the period's sharpest study of class and respectability.

title: Coming Up for Air
description: Orwell's finest novel: an insurance salesman returns to the childhood fishing pool and finds it built over.
plot_or_argument: George Bowling, a fat, forty-five-year-old insurance salesman, wins seventeen pounds on a horse and returns to the Thames Valley town of his childhood to fish in a secret pool — only to find the town swallowed by the suburbs and the pool become a rubbish tip. The novel ends with his realization that the war is coming.
narrative_structure: First-person narrative moving between 1938 and the childhood of 1900.
principal_characters: George Bowling; Hilda Bowling; Porteous; Old Porteous; Elsie
historical_context: The English suburbs of 1939, the motor road and the new housing estates, and the outbreak of the Second World War.
literary_significance: Coming Up for Air is Orwell's finest novel and the great English novel about the destruction of the countryside: its portrait of the suburb and the motor road, and its elegy for the Edwardian childhood, made it the period's most moving book about the loss of England.

title: The Road to Wigan Pier
description: Orwell's report on the industrial North: the coal mine, the dole, the tripe shop and the middle-class socialist.
plot_or_argument: The first half reports Orwell's investigations in Lancashire and Yorkshire in 1936: the lodgings, the coal face, the unemployment and the means test, the housing and the diet. The second half is a polemic against the English middle-class socialist, whose snobbery stands between the left and the working class.
narrative_structure: Two parts: a documentary report and a critical essay on socialism and class.
historical_context: The Depression of the 1930s, the means test, the Special Areas, the Jarrow March, and the Left Book Club that commissioned the book.
literary_significance: The Road to Wigan Pier is the finest English documentary book of the 1930s: its account of the coal face is one of the great passages of English reportage, and its second half is the period's sharpest critique of the left's own class prejudice.
